html:
Harriet Jacobs hid for almost seven years in a crawl space under the roof of her grandmother's house in Edenton, North Carolina. She was born into slavery and went into hiding in 1835 to escape the man who held her. Her two children lived in the house below and were not told she was there. She told the story in Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl (1861).

The garret was only nine feet long and seven wide. The highest part was three feet high, and sloped down abruptly to the loose board floor. There was no admission for either light or air. … To this hole I was conveyed as soon as I entered the house. The air was stifling; the darkness total. … The rats and mice ran over my bed; but I was weary, and I slept such sleep as the wretched may, when a tempest has passed over them.
Morning came. I knew it only by the noises I heard; for in my small den day and night were all the same. I suffered for air even more than for light. But I was not comfortless. I heard the voices of my children. There was joy and there was sadness in the sound. It made my tears flow. How I longed to speak to them! I was eager to look on their faces; but there was no hole, no crack, through which I could peep.

In 1842 she escaped to the North by boat. Her book came out in the first year of the American Civil War.
